This depends very strongly on what version of XP was used.

The plain old OEM version demands a product key. It also supposedly binds to the particular device (in this case, the motherboard swap would do it), in which case the original installation is useless and you may not be able to re-use the key.

Royalty OEM versions (e.g. Dell, HP, etc.) tend to detect the BIOS version for the specific manufacturer. These can bypass the activation process and just plain install. These discs can be reused on just about any machine from at least roughly the same time period, and maybe earlier or later. This is probably the easiest thing to do.

Retail upgrade and full versions also demand a product key. But they can be reused, so long as you aren't using them on more than one machine per copy. The system automatically deactivates if you change too many components during a given period of time, and will demand that you reactivate. This will often require calling a live phone number.

I suspect that the parent poster had the original OEM version. I'm also not sure that the product key was necessarily invalidated, and may in fact have been reusable to at least some degree. However, changing the motherboard, RAM and processor is definitely enough to trip the detection process to auto-invalidate. I think it happens when 3 of the major PC components changes within 6 months that it invalidates and demands reactivation; modern motherboards have a lot more than that, I'm sure. But it's been a long while since I read up on it.

hahahaha. This question I find... stupid? (I don't mean to be rude, really). You can have Linux, at any time. You don't have to ditch Windows regardless of how bad it is.
Let's face it, Windows, because of how popuiar it is, is a necessary evil at the moment. I don't use windows for much. Except for when I am playing something WINDOWS SPECIFIC (because even games like LoL, or WoW can be played through WINE on Linux) or writing software aimed for windows as well.

No, Linux is not "unbreakable", or "the safest", but it is very well optimised. Even Ubuntu (the most popuilar Linux Distro (Distro == Linux Flavor)) have disclaimers on their page (here) saying which weaknesses they can have in the OS, and they warn you about them, but because Linux has such "low" popularity, a lot of people who could be taking advantage of it, are not using it, which means that many of the threats that exist that are aimed at software, just like game developers who couldn't care less about Linux, are not AIMED at Linux users. That is an advantage.

The fact that Linux is founded in the FOSS (Free Open Source Software) Community, you can find SO MUCH software that replaces your "paid-for Windows counterparts" that can help you do exactly the same. (Microsoft Office < LibreOffice; Photoshop < Krita + GIMP; Windows Movie Maker/Sony Vegas/4D Cinema < Kdenlive/Blender; etc.) Of course, this software and its developers have their respective windows versions (mostly because they understand that software is from everyone to everyone, and they're happy to share it as much as they can, and is of awesome quality and support).

I am biased, yes, but I tried Linux for the first time by myself. It was scary, because NEW is always scary. I installed Ubuntu on an USB, tried it Live from the USB, liked it, installed it alongside windows, and have installed it in every computer I have had since. I recommend it more than anything else in this world. I still use windows, because like I said in the very beginning: IT IS A NECESSARY EVIL, but at the same time, A LOT OF PEOPLE don't need windows. A lot of people can find a lot more USER-FRIENDLY of POWER USER-Friendly flavours in Linux. Ubuntu, is the closest thing to windows you can have right now from the Linux community: It is an OS that even though is Linux, it has a certain degree of stability (a bit better than windows for me, but will never be close to Debian levels of Stability), and at the same time, it has companies/communities developing software for it, like BLEEDING EDGE levels of software. YES, you will still get to keep A LOT of the things you most likely already use in windows that would not be able to replace with Open Source counterparts. You will still be able to keep your Dropbox (because there's for Linux), you will still be able to keep Skype, you will keep your screen recording software (if you like recording games like me) with OBS, but the best part, is that if you are not supported, you might have a (VERY) slim chance to be able to use WINE/PlayOnLinux (read this for more info about it) to install or even run NAtive WINDOWS APPS!
There is just so much. It runs faster than me than windows does at the moment (I'm using Xubuntu, which is the Xfce desktop version of Ubuntu), and it is like a lightning in comparison to Windows.

If you are really planning to switch, I will give you a small list (tiny) for what I would recommend to you from the Linux community:
-If your focus is software (the latest), and want to keep up to date with everything, choose Ubuntu, which you can choose in some desktop flavours according to your needs:
* Kubuntu: Looks pretty (EXTREMELY PRETTY), but it is quite slow and resource heavy (just in comparison to the other ones)
* Ubuntu Gnome: VERY user-friendly. If you are have special "needs" like, you are hard of seeing or need accessibility tools most of all, and an easy User Interface.
* Ubuntu: quite user friendly, and pretty, but a somewhat weird environment for most Windows Refugees at first. Still, not a bad place to start.
* Xubuntu: EXTREMELY FAST and minimalistic. Very customisable as well (regarding keyboard shortcuts and all), but it doesn't have many visually "sparkling" features. But for me, it is what I need. Something simple, reliable, fast and customisable to my own taste.

If software is not your worry, and you worry more about the stability of your system, I recommend you go to Debian. It is the MOST stable of any OS out there, and one of the most popular choices of Linux "Experts" or Experienced Devs (It is Gabe Newel's favourite OS if I recall properly).

So just give some thought to it.

These were the words I originally wrote at the beginning of the minecraft forum post describing the Omen server, back when it was created. And these words may very well apply today, here on Voat. Welcome to the Omen server! Hopefully this server may bring you experiences that make up the Minecraft you love. The server is now at it's creation, or rather, its reincarnation.

History
The following is a text from the introduction originally written for Omen on the minecraftforums.net Jan 18th 2012:

Omen is a small community with mature and friendly members. Omen have existed since October 2011, but some of it's members have known each other long before that. The server running Omen is hosted by Cubedhost and owned by avantgeek. Over the years, the members of Omen has become good friends. By focusing on trust, friendship and lojality - we've come a long way with our server. The server is divided up by settlements, each with their own set of rules and governance. You can choose if you want to wander the woods alone, or help a settlement grow bigger. We're aiming for a more realistic and mature minecraft experience. Omen also got a set of friendly mature admins, and hopefully, you won't even notice that they really are admins.

Most of this is what I still want to apply to the server today.

 

Introduction
Hopefully we can build this up together. I have some sort of rules or rather ideas that I want to implement. I like Minecraft at it's Vanilla experience - I would like to continue this in the game. First it might be easier to list the things I don't want Omen to be;
--- Few/no mods
--- Few/no restrictions
--- No private chests
--- No invisible barriers
--- No private plots
--- No p2w
--- No "admin shop"
--- No donation gear/items

 

"But how do I protect myself from griefers?" You might say. The key to achieve this is to get to know the players that play. To see others. To make everyone have a more enjoyable experience without destroying things. Build up a community and include others.
I feel that on some servers with too many restrictions, friendships become rather monotone and entirely based on what we write to each other. In a server with no such restriction, I know that my friend is my friend both because we hit it off in the chat and because he doesn't destroy my stuff. The game kinda becomes more meaningful.

 

There will almost always be that one griefer who doesn't care. We could make an application and whitelist system, from previous experience, this works pretty well but still has some downsides; Some people have a short attention span. They see a server and want to test it out right away. They might not take the time to write an application just to test out a server. They might be really cool people, unfortunately we could lose them by making them write an application. Therefore I have another idea. I don't think it's original but either way it might be worth trying out: At the spawn there will be an obstacle course of sorts. A set of obstacles both psychological and in-game physical. Quizzes, puzzles and parkour obstacles. By completing it, you have become a member of the server. This would a sort of dynamic application prossess. More efficient, including and enjoyable. By becoming a member by mastering a set of obstacles you wouldn't want to throw all the hard work away by just griefing.

 

One of the thing I loved with Minecraft is the possibility to create settlements, towns and cities. Make a governance, discuss town rules. The administrative bit. A sort of roleplay experience if you want. I also loved the competitive. Making arenas and gamemodes. A keyword in this is "controlled competition". I think some of this reflect in the following things I would like in a server:
--- No griefing
--- Semi-hardcore mode
Your death would result in you spawning I a sort of purgatory where you have to complete a parkour course/puzzle to be spawned back into the world again.
--- Competitions
Arena matches/controlled battles
--- Mystical Intrusions
After a while create quests/special worlds
--- Balance A very bad thing for servers is too much admin interference. Admins building stuff and ruining the block worth for others. Admins spawning stuff. Teleporting players. A thing that has worked before is to make the admins almost invicible, that way everyone feel more included I think.

 

The Plan
The most important thing about the server is you. So I want us to shape this together. In the future we'll have some polls and discussions on how we should do things. Though I do have a short road map here so you get the general idea of what needs to be done.

[✔] - Make this post
[  ] - Measure interest
[✔] - Buy the server
[✔] - Enable whitelist
[  ] - Make a list of members
[  ] - Post a set of rules
[  ] - Create "The Choosing" (the spawn obstacle course)
[  ] - Disable whitelist after The Choosing have been created
[  ] - Find more things I could add to this road map

 

For now I have applied whitelist. I need people to help me out with the The Choosing!

How I managed to get the banner to fit how I want it to for my subverse.

Great work, thesladenator. The sub looks really good.

The reason I suggest not modifying the base CSS is because it makes it difficult to update to the latest version when a new one is released. If you were to place your custom CSS below the base, it becomes a matter of copying and pasting in order to update Scribble, making it far easier than having to copy and paste, then remember what changes you made to it in the first place so you can make those same changes.

But it looks good, and I may have to request a banner in the future. Great work.

Thank you! Its taken me three days trying multiple methods and reading through comments suggesting ideas etc to get it right. I understand that it will make it difficult for updates and such but it works for now and I'm happy about that! I'm still learning CSS and HTML so one day I might come back to it and change it with everything below the base, but for now I'm leaving it like this. I only posted this because I've seen a lot of comments where people have tried to get the banners to fit right as well as discussion about the actual size of the banner, of course this won't be a permanent solution because of the updates.

I completely get it. I really should make it easier for people to get the right size for the banner. I'll add that as a mention on the customization tool, and hopefully that will work better. Thanks for your work with Scribble.

BTW, in order to have the image the way you wanted it to be, and place the code at the bottom, you would just need to place the following code at the bottom of the CSS field:

#header {
 background-size: contain;
}

Having it at the bottom of the CSS means that it will take priority over any other rule that comes before it (except ones that have the !important designation). That said, it never occurred to me that people would want to contain a background image, instead of use it to cover the area, so that's a unique way of using it; it works really well, especially in this case, so it may be something I think about in the future. Keep going with learning CSS, it's a lot of fun and it makes for some really cool things. You're doing really well so far, in being able to change that specific bit of code. Background-size is generally one of the later things people learn, so you're on the right track.
